Sheung Shui recorded 39.8 degrees

At 3 p.m. and 4 p.m., Sheung Shui recorded 39.8 degrees, the highest temperature in Hong Kong since automatic weather stations were set up in the 1980s. At the Hong Kong Observatory, the highest temperature recorded was 36.9 degrees, the highest since records began in 1884. Yuen Long Park, Ta Kwu Ling, Happy Valley and others recorded 37.3 degrees; Tseung Kwan O 36.9 degrees; Sham Shui Po 36.5 degrees.

Issuing work warnings based on the Hong Kong Heat Index. According to the Labour Department's guidelines, the Labour Department issues work heatstroke warnings based on the Hong Kong Heat Index measured by the Hong Kong Observatory at King's Park. When the Hong Kong Heat Index reaches 30 to 32, a yellow work heatstroke warning is issued, indicating that heat stress in some work environments is considerably high. When it reaches 32 to 34, a red warning is issued, indicating that heat stress in some work environments is very high. When the index reaches 34, a black warning is issued, indicating that heat stress in some work environments is extremely high.

Only reached yellow warning standard. Although today's temperature broke a record of more than a hundred years, the Hong Kong Observatory's Hong Kong Heat Index at 3 p.m. was only 31.3, merely reaching the yellow warning standard. The Labour Department's guidelines also point out that if other monitoring stations show that heat stress in many locations in Hong Kong has reached a certain level, even if the index at King's Park has not reached that level, the Labour Department will still issue the corresponding work heatstroke warning.

What is the Hong Kong Heat Index? The Hong Kong Heat Index is a heat stress index developed by the Hong Kong Observatory in collaboration with the Faculty of Medicine at CUHK, based on the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) index. It incorporates meteorological data such as ambient temperature, humidity, air movement and solar heat radiation levels, as well as the overall hospital admission figures in Hong Kong for consideration.

Never seen red or black since its launch?

Since the work heatstroke warning was launched in 2023, red and black warnings have never been issued. According to records, from May 15, 2023 to July 31 this year, a total of 199 work heatstroke warnings were issued, all of which were yellow.

Labour Department: But relative humidity was low and wind conditions were favourable. In response to enquiries, the Labour Department said that although today's (9th) temperature was particularly high, relative humidity was lower than usual summer conditions, and with favourable wind conditions, the Hong Kong Heat Index measured by the Observatory at ten locations today mostly ranged from 30 to less than 32. The Labour Department therefore issued a yellow heatstroke warning in accordance with the mechanism.

Warning issued if four or more of the nine monitoring stations reach the threshold

The Labour Department also said that the Observatory published heat index data for more areas in April this year. Since April 20, the Labour Department has further enhanced the Work Heatstroke Warning system by incorporating heat index data from more areas as criteria for issuing Work Heatstroke Warnings. In addition to continuing to use the Hong Kong Heat Index data measured at King's Park, data from nine other locations has also been added as criteria for issuing Work Heatstroke Warnings.

The Labour Department said that if four or more of the other nine Hong Kong Heat Index monitoring stations show that heat stress in multiple locations in Hong Kong has reached a certain level, even if the King's Park index has not reached that level, the Labour Department will still issue the corresponding Work Heatstroke Warning. The Labour Department said it will closely monitor hot weather and the operation of the Work Heatstroke Warning system, and review whether the system needs further enhancement.

Referring to temperature, humidity, air movement and heat radiation data

The Labour Department added that the Hong Kong Heat Index is a heat stress index jointly developed by the Hong Kong Observatory and the Faculty of Medicine at CUHK, based on the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature index. Its calculation method is similar to the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature, incorporating meteorological data such as ambient temperature, humidity, air movement and solar heat radiation levels, together with Hong Kong's overall hospital admission figures for consideration. It can appropriately reflect the health risks to the general public in Hong Kong arising from heat stress.

Labour Department: Temperature is only one of the risk factors

The Labour Department emphasised that temperature is only one of the risk factors for heat stress, along with others such as humidity, wind speed and solar radiation. The Labour Department has always advocated using the Guidelines rather than relying solely on temperature as the criterion for assessing heat stress risk.

The Labour Department also pointed out that if an employee suffers injury or death during the course of employment (including injury or death caused by work-related heat stress incidents), the employer is liable for compensation. Whether a case constitutes a work injury and whether the employer is liable for employees' compensation must be considered based on the facts and specific circumstances of each individual case, as well as the objective environment, and cannot be generalised.
